puerile

/PYOOR-ul/ - the stress falls on PYOOR · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Puerile means juvenile, immature.

Forty years on, the twins' puerile ritual survives: whoever says 'jinx' first owns the other's dessert.

Worked Example

The film critic spent four paragraphs dismissing the blockbuster's humor as puerile — food fights, rude noises, a fart joke with a sequel — and one closing sentence confessing he had laughed twice.

Puerile is a judgment, not a description of age: it scolds grown people for humor or conduct that belongs in a school corridor. A child's silliness is just childish; it earns puerile only when someone old enough to know better keeps it up.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

childish: Childish means acting like a child, and anyone can say it — warmly of a game, sharply of a coworker. Puerile is the critic's colder version: it always passes judgment, scolding grown people for conduct beneath their age. A birthday party can be happily childish; only a fault is puerile.

sophomoric: Sophomoric mocks immaturity that thinks itself clever — the smug dorm-room philosopher, jokes proud of their own daring. Puerile is the plainer judgment: conduct or humor that is simply juvenile, with no pretension of sophistication required. Sophomoric faults the self-satisfaction; puerile faults the immaturity itself.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

grown-up: behaving like the adult in the room

sensible: governed by good judgment

Where it sits · how young the conduct seems — silly → puerile → infantile

silly vs. puerile: Silly is milder than puerile — light foolishness that nobody needs to outgrow.

infantile vs. puerile: Infantile is harsher than puerile: puerile conduct belongs on a playground, while infantile conduct belongs in a crib.

Which word fits?

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — puer

Root — puer: boy, child (Latin)

Suffix — -ile

Suffix — -ile: of, like (adjective ending)

Put it together

Put it together: Puer (boy, child) + -ile (of, like) = boy-like. Latin puerilis simply meant 'of a child,' no insult intended; English kept the shape and sharpened the point, so that puerile now scolds adults for behavior their twelve-year-old selves should have retired.

Why there's no relative to spot

Why there's no relative to spot: Latin puer, 'boy,' fathered almost nothing else in common English — puerility is just this word's own noun, and the rest of the family stayed behind in Latin. Puerile stands alone, fittingly for a word about refusing to grow.

Strength Check

Word Choice

formal / dismissive

Puerile is the critic's word for immaturity — cooler and more cutting than childish, which anyone might say warmly of a game. Its unit neighbor petulance names one specific immature display, the sulk; puerile passes judgment on the whole performance. Save infantile for when you want the insult absolute.
